hero.eyebrow: v0.2.0 · open source · runs on your hardware
hero.title: Run the agents you love.
hero.lede: AI agents you know and love on secure, high-performance rails. Run everything you need on a small computer like the Raspberry Pi.
hero.caveat: 17 public Rust crates, three CLIs, a separate permission broker, sandboxed agent tools, and OpenTelemetry built in.

title: Everything you need.
Nothing running wild.
pillars.intro: Version 0.2.0 brings isolation, exact authorization, pluggable I/O, auditing, and telemetry—all in a stack small enough to run beside your agents on a Raspberry Pi.

items.title: Built for your hardware.
items.body: Run Dekopon with Rust binaries, plain files, Unix sockets, and Wasm. There is no required cloud service. The project already runs beside OpenObserve on a Raspberry Pi.

items.title: Fine-grained capabilities.
items.body: Stay in control with permissioned I/O, hard runtime limits, and deny-by-default rules. Read and write access stay separate, and each approval is tied to one action.

items.title: Bring your own tools.
items.body: Add custom Rust providers without filling the prompt with tool definitions. Your agent gets one familiar scripting tool and sees only the capabilities you grant.

items.title: Know what happened.
items.body: Audit records show what the broker approved. Traces show where time went. Logs keep costs, refusals, errors, and any transcripts you explicitly choose to record.

status.title: Get running in less than 5 minutes.
status.intro: Install the CLI from crates.io and start on hardware you already own. The release includes 17 crates, three command-line tools, attested binaries, and end-to-end tests.

current.label: Your agent runtime
current.title: One tool gives the agent everything you allow.
current.body: Connect an OpenAI-compatible model or an isolated ChatGPT/Codex account. The agent can then combine approved capabilities in one sandboxed script.
points: One tool definition, no matter how many capabilities you add
Loops, functions, pipelines, and real jq for structured data
No access to processes, files, or your environment
Fresh Wasm sandboxes with memory, time, input, and output limits
Local Chrome traces or standard OpenTelemetry export

direction.label: Permissioned I/O
direction.title: Your agent asks. The broker checks.
direction.body: A separate local service verifies who is asking, checks an exact allow/deny rule, limits the network request, blocks replays, and records the result.

items.name: Fine-grained rules
items.description: who, which agent, which capability, which provider

items.name: Hard I/O limits
items.description: destination, method, calls, bytes, and time

direction.note: Still to come: broker-managed provider credentials, independently anchored audit checkpoints, a long-running agent service, and multi-tenant networking.

execution.title: One tool. A complete plan.
execution.intro: Your agent can discover, combine, and reuse the capabilities you allow in a single call. You get fewer model round trips without giving the model a real operating-system shell.
execution.script:
items=$(cap --list)
for item in $items; do
  cap --describe $item | jq -c .inputSchema
done
execution.result: structured JSON · limited output · clear exit codes

cards.title: One stable interface
cards.body: Add or remove providers without changing the model’s tool schema. The agent discovers only the capabilities available in this session.

cards.title: Structured from start to finish
cards.body: Variables and pipelines carry JSON values. Arrays, maps, arithmetic, and jq work without repeatedly turning data into text.

cards.title: No access to your OS
cards.body: The interpreter cannot start programs, read files, open sockets, inherit environment variables, or run eval. It only reaches capabilities you grant.

cards.title: Limits at every layer
cards.body: Steps, memory, output, runtime, recursion, and tool calls are capped. Each Wasm provider and broker request has its own limits too.

authority.title: Your agent can ask.
authority.intro: Every outside action crosses a separate permission boundary. The broker verifies the local caller, checks the exact rule and limits, then approves one use. The agent cannot approve itself.

nodes.title: Request
nodes.body: The agent asks for one named capability with limited JSON input. It cannot include its own identity or permission.

nodes.title: Permission check
nodes.body: The broker verifies the local caller, blocks replays, checks the exact rule, and approves one use.

nodes.title: Limited provider
nodes.body: The provider starts in a fresh Wasm sandbox. Dekopon limits its destination, methods, call count, bytes, memory, and time.

nodes.title: Audit record
nodes.body: The final record ties the verified identity, decision, safe request details, result, and trace together.

invariants.title: Read does not mean write
invariants.body: Every action has its own capability. Permission to fetch a post never grants permission to create one.

invariants.title: Identity comes from the OS
invariants.body: The model cannot type in a different identity. The broker gets local identity from the connection and your configuration.

invariants.title: Power stays in the broker
invariants.body: The runner never receives the broker’s approval object and never loads the privileged network interface.

invariants.title: Failures tell you what to do
invariants.body: Dekopon distinguishes work that never started from work that may have happened but could not be recorded.

observability.title: See what your agent did.
observability.intro: Follow a run from model prompt to broker and provider. OpenTelemetry works with OpenObserve and other standard backends, while the broker keeps its own durable audit trail.

signals.name: Audit trail
signals.question: What was allowed?
signals.body: An owner-only, hash-linked file records each decision and result. The broker checks it again when it starts.

signals.name: Traces
signals.question: Where did time go?
signals.body: See model turns, scripts, commands, permission checks, provider work, and safe HTTP details in one cross-process trace.

signals.name: Logs
signals.question: What should we keep?
signals.body: Keep token usage, costs, refusals, errors, and optional transcripts without duplicating every trace span.

observability.privacyBody: Prompts, answers, scripts, tool output, provider data, URL paths, headers, bodies, credentials, and raw errors stay out by default. You can opt selected transcript data into telemetry; secrets and durable audit payloads stay out.

measurement.label: Raspberry Pi · OpenObserve · real disk use
measurement.title: for the current Dekopon sample
measurement.body: The Dekopon sample on the project Raspberry Pi uses 148 KiB for traces and 52 KiB for logs. These are physical blocks on disk, not sparse-file estimates.
measurement.note: Measured 16 Aug 2026. This is an aggregate sample, not a fixed cost per prompt. The full OpenObserve stream tree used 1.22 MiB, including indexes and metadata.

resources.title: Permissions live in plain files.
resources.intro: Describe agents, capabilities, and providers in compact YAML or JSON. Dekopon rejects unknown fields and broken references before your agent runs.

points.label: key
points.title: Credential names
points.body: stand in for secret values in shared config.

points.label: sort
points.title: Predictable output
points.body: stays easy to read and automate.

resources.yaml:
apiVersion: dekopon.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: reviewer
spec:
  description: Reviews pull requests
  capabilities:
    - github.pull-request.read
    - github.pull-request.comment
status: Ready
resources.terminal:
$ dekopon get agents -o wide

NAME       ENABLED   CAPABILITIES   STATUS
reviewer   true      2              Ready
snooper    false     1              Disabled

$ dekopon validate
✓ configuration is valid

architecture.title: Each part has one job.
architecture.intro: Pure local tools run without network access. Outside actions go through a separate broker that owns permissions, limits, and audit. The agent never inherits that power.

current.title: Simple local control
current.body: Check configuration, inspect agents, and manage model login from one predictable CLI.

components.title: Agent runner
components.body: Talks to the model, runs the one-tool sandbox, and asks the broker for outside actions.

components.title: Permission broker
components.body: Verifies identity, checks rules, limits I/O, and records every decision and result.

components.title: Custom provider
components.body: Runs one approved operation in a fresh sandbox with only the host features it needs.

roadmap.title: Built honestly, one layer at a time.
roadmap.intro: Version 0.2.0 proves the local permission path. Next comes safer credential handling, stronger audit retention, and a smoother path from agent config to execution.

items.title: Local agent configuration
items.body: Strict resources, predictable CLI output, model clients, and pure Wasm providers.

items.title: Secure local execution
items.body: One-tool scripting, permissioned HTTP, replay protection, durable audit, and cross-process telemetry.

items.title: Stronger audit anchoring
items.body: Keep signed or remote checkpoint copies outside the broker host.

items.title: Broker-managed credentials
items.body: Inject destination-bound secrets without exposing them to agents or provider code.

items.title: Long-running agent service
items.body: Connect agent configuration to continuous execution without moving permissions into the runner.

closing.title: Run agents on your terms.
closing.body: Install Dekopon, bring a model and your own tools, and see how far secure self-hosted agents can go on hardware you already own.
